item.title: AVS, the delay on reforms: Economiesuisse's alarm
item.description: Mäder, outgoing President Economiesuisse, criticizes the government: discussion on the postponed retirement age, risks to the sustainability of the system.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Mäder criticizes government: too late on crucial AVS reforms - Retirement age: political taboo, government avoids discussion - Demographic: increasingly serious imbalance between taxpayers and pensioners
## Key facts - **What**: Outgoing President Economiesuisse criticises lack of reforms - When: Recent interview at Tages-Anzeiger - Where: Switzerland, national context - Who: Christoph Mäder (67 years old), former Sandoz and Novartis - Topic: AVS and Swiss social security sustainability
Christoph Mäder raises his voice at the end of his six-year term as President of Economiesuisse. In an interview with Tages-Anzeiger, the 67-year-old is blunt: Switzerland is losing competitiveness to international rivals, and the onus is on the Federal Council's lack of political will to tackle indispensable structural reforms. Mäder, a lawyer and former executive at Sandoz and Novartis, will soon be replaced by Silvan Wildhaber.
The main target of his criticism is the AVS, the Swiss pension system that represents the first pillar of national security. Mäder is very harsh in judging the government's decision to exclude from the next AVS reform any discussion of raising the retirement age:
> “I consider it irresponsible, to use a cautious adjective, to decide not to even discuss retirement age in the upcoming AVS reform.”

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Practical Steps: What Cross-Border Workers Should Do
The alarm raised by Mäder, however critical, should not paralyze the cross-border worker: on the contrary, it is all the more reason to prepare actively. Early retirement planning, a prudent scenario that considers possible reforms of the AVS system, diversification between the first and third pillar—all of this reduces the risk of unpleasant surprises at the time of retirement. Those who start planning today have time to adapt to possible changes tomorrow.
### First Step: Verify Your AVS Contribution Status
The first step is to know your contribution history. Every cross-border worker G can request a free copy of the AVS account statement from the compensation fund responsible for the Ticino canton or through the Swiss social security online portal. The statement shows years of contributions accumulated, amounts paid (both employee and employer portions), any contribution gaps, and an estimate of the monthly AVS pension at age 65 (current standard).
This verification is essential to understand your position: how many years remain until retirement, whether there is room to improve your pension, which gaps to fill to maximize future benefits. A careful analysis of your personal file enables realistic planning.
### Specialized Advice for Cross-Border Workers
Given the complexity of the system—which combines Swiss regulations, the 1976 Italian-Swiss tax treaty, the new cross-border agreement in force since January 1, 2024, and possible rights accrued in the Italian system—it is advisable to seek advice from a qualified advisor in cross-border matters. A specialized professional can analyze your personal file (years of Swiss contributions, any Italian contributions, gaps), simulate scenarios with the current retirement age vs. increased age (if the reform is approved), and suggest optimization strategies for the third pillar (pillar 3a) to compensate for any future reductions in AVS.
### Monitor Regulatory Developments
Mäder observes that the government is postponing the discussion on retirement age, but this does not mean that the reform is permanently blocked. It is advisable to stay informed about federal messages, public consultations on AVS reforms, statements from federations like Economiesuisse, and changes in contribution rates (the current 5.3% could increase over time). Constant vigilance on the regulatory front is a tool of protection.
### Evaluate Early or Delayed Retirement
Switzerland allows you to claim AVS starting from an age below 65 (with reductions in the pension) or to defer beyond 65 (receiving increases in the monthly benefit). In the context of uncertainty described by Mäder, the cross-border worker could evaluate both scenarios:
- **Early Retirement**: if you have accumulated a good contribution history, you could decide to retire earlier, accepting a permanent reduction in your pension. This offers greater flexibility in choosing the timing.
- Delayed Retirement: if you want to maximize your pension and have the health to continue, you can work beyond age 65, receiving increases in your monthly benefit. Each additional year of work increases both the contributions paid and the duration of pension payments.
Both scenarios have pros and cons that depend on your personal situation, life expectancy, expected medical costs, and desire for retirement.
### Use the Frontaliere Ticino Online Calculator
The Frontaliere Ticino website offers a [specialized pension calculator](nav:calculator) for cross-border workers that allows you to simulate expected AVS pension at age 65, the effect of a possible increase in retirement age, calculation of early/delayed pension, and integration with the professional pillar if known. This tool, updated with the latest regulations, is one of the fastest ways to get a realistic estimate of your Swiss pension and to compare different scenarios.

item.title: Living in Mesenzana and working in Ticino
item.description: Learn how to live in Mesenzana and work in Ticino as a border worker: permits, taxation, transport, cost of living and procedures. Practical guide.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Mesenzana is a few kilometers from the Ticino border, accessible via Brogeda and Gaggiolo - G frontier workers declare income in Italy (INPS) and pay taxes in Switzerland - LAMal is compulsory; new frontier workers have a declarative allowance of €10'000 - Cost of living lower than in Ticino, but services and infrastructures are more limited
## Key facts
- **What**: Living in Mesenzana and working in Ticino as a frontier worker - Where: Mesenzana (province of Varese), border with Canton Ticino - Who: Frontier workers with G or B permit - Regulatory agreement: New Frontier Workers Agreement (in force since 1 January 2024) - Allowance: €10'000 for new frontier workers, €7'500 for existing ones (2024‑2033) - Main crossings: Brogeda, Gaggiolo
Mesenzana, an Italian municipality in the province of Varese, attracts a growing number of frontier workers who work in the Canton of Ticino. A short distance from the Brogeda and Gaggiolo crossings, it offers quick access to the main Ticino economic centres — Lugano, Mendrisio, Chiasso — while maintaining a lower cost of living compared to the Swiss side.
Choosing to reside in Mesenzana while working in Ticino entails, however, a series of specific administrative and fiscal obligations. G permit frontier workers must register with INPS in Italy and declare employment income, while the withholding tax is retained exclusively in Switzerland by the employer. The new Italy‑Switzerland tax agreement — in force since 1 January 2024 — significantly affects these obligations. Before moving, one must assess the overall picture of rights and duties.
### Geographic situation and access to crossings
Mesenzana lies a short distance from the Ticino border. The main accesses to Ticino are via the Brogeda crossing, the main road linking the Varese Valley to Ticino, and the Gaggiolo crossing. The strategic location enables reaching the main Ticino economic poles in reasonable time, although exact travel times depend on the final destination in Ticino and traffic flow at the crossings — factors that condition the daily commuter’s planning.
Anyone living in Mesenzana and working in Ticino falls fully under the frontier worker regime. The implications are both administrative and fiscal: obligation to register with INPS, respecting the days of presence in Italy to maintain frontier worker status, and adherence to Italian declaration regimes. Moreover, it will be necessary to evaluate the health‑insurance option (Swiss LAMal or Italian SSN) and understand the pension implications (AVS, LPP, unemployment insurance).
### The New Frontier Workers Agreement and fiscal implications
The New Frontier Workers Agreement — signed on 23 December 2020 and ratified in Italy by Law 83 of 13 June 2023, entering into force on 1 January 2024 — introduced significant changes to the tax regime. New frontier workers, i.e. those who acquired this status from 17 July 2023 onwards, have a declarative allowance of €10'000 per year. Those who were already frontier workers before that date benefit from an exemption of €7'500, with a transitional regime foreseen until 2033.
This agreement represents an important evolution compared with the previous regime, as it simplifies certain declaration obligations and improves tax predictability for new commuters. However, anyone moving from Mesenzana to work in Ticino must understand the mechanism of the Italy‑Switzerland Convention against Double Taxation (signed 9 December 1976) and how the tax credit applicable in the CE section of the Italian 730 tax return recovers the taxes paid in Switzerland. ### Taxation and declaratory obligations
The tax system for those who reside in Mesenzana and work in Ticino follows precise rules. In Italy, the border worker is required to register with INPS as an employee and to file an annual tax return (Form 730 or Income Tax). However, the declared income is taxed exclusively in Switzerland, where the employer applies the tax at source. To avoid double taxation, Italy recognises a tax credit — indicated in the EC framework of declaration 730 — which allows taxes paid in Switzerland to be recovered.
The structure of the Swiss paycheck for a frontier worker includes deductions for:
- **AVS/AI/IPG** (old-age and disability insurance): 5.3% to be paid by the employee - Unemployment (AD) and accident (AC) insurance: 1.1% up to CHF 148'200 of income - LAINF (accident insurance): 0.7–1.5% - LPP (pension fund according to pillar): 7–18% depending on the age group (from 25 years) - Cantonal/municipal source tax: withheld as a percentage of gross income
In Italy, on the other hand, the border worker pays:
- INPS (social security contributions): percentage calculated by the Swiss employer on a bilateral basis - IRPEF (Personal Income Tax): progressive rates from 23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001 and €50,000, 43% over €50,000

## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Pre-transfer Checklist
Before moving to Mesenzana and starting a frontier worker activity in Ticino, it is advisable to check some key points:
1. **Employment Contract**: Ensure that the Swiss employer is willing to offer a frontier worker contract with the appropriate deductions and communications to INPS.
2. Frontier Worker Permit (Permit G): Request the permit from the competent local Italian authority (municipality of Mesenzana) in coordination with the Swiss SEM (State Secretariat for Migration). The procedure varies depending on the destination canton for work.
3. Registration with INPS: Once hired, register with INPS as a frontier worker employee. The Swiss employer will submit contribution data in a bilateral scheme.
4. LAMal or SSN Choice: Decide within the established deadlines whether to keep Italian health insurance (free SSN) or switch to Swiss LAMal (with monthly premium).
5. Tax and Accounting Tracking: Prepare a system to keep Swiss pay slips, Italian tax declarations, and expense invoices (especially if you intend to seek deductions for commuting costs — although their deductibility depends on the applicable Italian regime).
6. Residence and Notifications: Register your change of residence at the Mesenzana municipality and notify INPS within 30 days.
### Tools and Available Resources
Our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to estimate your monthly net income considering Italian (INPS) and Swiss deductions (AVS, LPP, LAMal, source tax). By entering your Swiss gross salary, you can see the impact of both tax systems and plan a realistic monthly budget.
For an in-depth analysis of double taxation effects and available tax refunds, see our guide on [tax refunds](nav:ristorni). Additionally, the [cost of living comparison](nav:cost-of-living) tool for Ticino-Italy will help you quantify the actual economic advantage of moving to Mesenzana.
Before purchasing health insurance, consult our page on [LAMal and health insurance](nav:health) to compare options between Swiss LAMal and Italian SSN based on your family situation. Use our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate your monthly net income considering the LAMal-SSN choice and plan your move with complete tax awareness.

item.title: The book about the border worker boom in Switzerland
item.description: New academic book explains how Switzerland has 400,000 frontier workers. From 84,000 in 1978 to the boom after 2000. Focus on wages, taxation, transport.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Switzerland with 400,000+ cross-border workers: first European country by number - An academic book explains the boom: from 84,000 in 1978 to today - Three areas absorb 80%: French-speaking Switzerland, Ticino, Basel cantons - Topics addressed: wages, taxation, transport, xenophobia, social security
## Key facts - **What**: Publication of the book 'Le travail frontalier en Suisse – 30 questions' (Alphil) - When: Recent release; acceleration since 2000 (EU-CH free movement agreement) - Where: Switzerland; focus on 3 geographical areas (80% of cross-border workforce) - Who: Authors: Stéphane Rossini, Jean-Claude Rennwald, Daniel Droz, Alexandre Moine - Number: 400,000 cross-border workers today vs 84,000 in 1978 (5x growth in ~50 years)
### The cross-border worker boom in numbers
Switzerland has become the European country employing the largest number of cross-border workers. In 1978, following the 1974-75 economic crisis, there were 84,000. Today, they exceed 400,000. This jump was not linear, but underwent a decisive acceleration after 2000, the year the agreement on the free movement of persons between Switzerland and the European Union came into force — also favored by the robustness of the Swiss economy.
A new book, titled 'Le travail frontalier en Suisse – 30 questions' and published by Alphil editions, aims to clarify a continuously growing phenomenon: debunking myths and analyzing challenges and opportunities through statistical data and answers to key questions. In public debate, the phenomenon of cross-border workers is often at the center of controversy and misunderstanding.
### The authors and academic expertise
The book is authored by four experts of international standing: Stéphane Rossini (former Socialist National Councilor from Valais, former director of the Federal Social Insurance Office), Jean-Claude Rennwald (former National Councilor from Jura and trade unionist), Daniel Droz (journalist from Arcinfo), and Alexandre Moine (geographer). This combination of political, union, journalistic, and geographical expertise allows for a 360-degree analysis of the phenomenon.
The work focuses on the three geographical areas that alone absorb over 80% of the cross-border workforce: French-speaking Switzerland, Ticino, and the two cantons of Basel. In these regions, cross-border work is structural to the local economy and the relationship with neighboring countries. The themes covered in the volume range from economic aspects to social and infrastructural issues: employment, wages, social dumping, social security, taxation, vocational training, housing availability, spatial planning, transport, teleworking, and the delicate relationship between cross-border workers and resident workers, as well as between states and European authorities. ### The three key areas: geographical concentration and reasons
The concentration of border workers in three specific areas — French Switzerland, Ticino, Basel — is no coincidence. These regions benefit from geographical proximity to neighbouring countries, a robust local economy, and a historical tradition of cross-border economic exchanges. Ticino, in particular, serves as a bridge to the Italian Lombard economy. French Switzerland overlooks France, while Basel borders France and Germany.
This geographical concentration creates challenges common to all three areas: infrastructural pressure on border crossings, traffic congestion, coordination needs between health and social security systems, and local debates on competition in labour markets.
### Contemporary challenges: from social dumping to xenophobia
The book addresses issues crucial to the daily life of the border worker. A first area concerns wages and social dumping: are frontier workers really paid less than resident workers? To what extent does their inflow affect local Swiss wages?
Social security is another priority. How does health insurance, the AVS (old-age pension) and the second pillar (LPP) work for those who work in Switzerland but reside in Italy? These issues directly affect the protection of the border worker during their working life.
Traffic is a recurring theme in the public debate on border crossers. ### Dove trovare il libro e come approfondire
Il libro "Le travail frontalier en Suisse – 30 questions" è pubblicato dalle edizioni Alphil, un editore specializzato in scienze sociali e umanistiche con sede in Svizzera romanda. È possibile ordinarlo tramite i principali canali di vendita libraria online e presso le librerie specializzate in saggistica economica e sociale.
Per il frontaliere, questa pubblicazione rappresenta una risorsa preziosa per comprendere il contesto normativo, economico e sociale in cui opera. Leggerla significa acquisire una visione d'insieme delle sfide collettive — e non solo individuali — che caratterizzano il lavoro transfrontaliero. Non è soltanto una questione personale di busta paga o dichiarazione fiscale, ma di comprensione critica del fenomeno nel quale sei inserito.
### Approfondire i tuoi diritti: strumenti pratici
Accanto a questa lettura, è importante padroneggiare alcuni aspetti concreti della vita da frontaliere. Il tuo stipendio in Svizzera è calcolato secondo regole specifiche, così come i contributi sociali (AVS, secondo pilastro LPP, assicurazione malattia). Le tasse e gli ristorni seguono convenzioni bilaterali tra Svizzera e Italia.
Puoi verificare in autonomia come il tuo reddito lordo si trasforma in netto utilizzando il [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) del nostro sito. Questo strumento ti aiuta a capire l'impatto reale di contributi e imposte sulla tua busta paga, mese dopo mese.
Se cerchi un nuovo lavoro oltre confine o desideri monitorare le opportunità nel mercato frontaliero, gli [annunci di lavoro](nav:jobs) specializzati in questo segmento raccolgono proposte da aziende ticinesi e svizzere che assumono attivamente frontalieri.
### Protezione dalla disoccupazione e gestione fiscale
Un altro aspetto affrontato dal libro è il rapporto tra frontalieri e precarietà occupazionale. Se il tuo contratto venisse risolto, come funziona l'assicurazione contro la disoccupazione? Quali diritti hai? Per comprendere meglio questo tema, consulta la sezione dedicata alla [disoccupazione per frontalieri](nav:unemployment) sul nostro sito.
Altrettanto cruciale è la [dichiarazione dei redditi](nav:tax-return): un passaggio obbligatorio annuale che richiede attenzione ai dettagli per versamenti, ritenute e crediti d'imposta. Una guida specializzata può fare la differenza nella gestione corretta della tua posizione fiscale. Non lasciare il tuo futuro finanziario al caso. Accedi oggi stesso al [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) e verifica quanto stai effettivamente guadagnando dopo tutti i prelievi.
*Source: [swissinfo.ch](https://www.swissinfo.ch/ita/frontalieri%3a-ecco-il-libro-che-spiega-il-boom-avvenuto-in-svizzera/92024342)*

item.title: S30 blocked between Cadenazzo and Luino due to technical failure
item.description: Railway line interrupted until Wednesday 9 September 2026 at 4:00 am. Replacement buses available but with guaranteed delays and no connections.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- S30 line completely blocked between Cadenazzo and Luino due to technical failure of the railway system - Extended interruption until Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 4:00 AM - Replacement buses in service with no guarantee of connections - Cross-border workers advised to check information before departure and add 30-45 minutes to travel time
## Key facts
- **What**: Complete interruption of railway traffic on the S30 line - Where: Route Cadenazzo (Ticino) – Luino (Italy, Lombardy) - When: Until Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 4:00 AM - Cause: Technical failure of the railway system - Temporary solution: Replacement buses with possible delays
---
Railway traffic on the S30 line between Cadenazzo and Luino is completely interrupted. A technical failure of the railway system has made it impossible for trains to circulate on the cross-border route. The interruption will continue at least until Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 4:00 AM, directly affecting cross-border workers who depend on this connection to reach their workplace in Lombardy.
To ensure a minimum connection between Ticino and Italy, replacement bus services have been arranged. However, the situation remains complicated: passengers have been explicitly advised to account for significant waiting times and possible delays. A particularly important warning: connections cannot be guaranteed. This means that those relying on coordinated transfers between different means of transport could find themselves stranded for long periods at stations.
### The impact on cross-border mobility
For cross-border workers who daily cross the border for work purposes, the loss of the S30 line is not a simple inconvenience. It is a disruption to routine. Those who regularly use the train have structured their schedules around railway punctuality: departure at 6:45 AM, arrival at 7:30 AM, shift start at 8:00 AM. With replacement buses, the same journey could take 75-90 minutes, making it impossible to maintain usual schedules. Anyone traveling between Ticino and Luino must check information shortly before departure and plan for extra travel time — these are not theoretical suggestions, but a concrete necessity to avoid risking being late at work. ## How the service disruption affects cross-border commuters
The S30 line disruption directly impacts those who have built a mobility routine on this route. For many cross-border commuters, deciding how to travel over the next two days is not straightforward. The replacement bus is available, but requires rigid planning: waiting times at stops are predictable, but bus schedules do not perfectly align with the train schedules they are meant to replace. Those accustomed to reading the newspaper during their train commute will instead need to find a seat on a potentially crowded bus.
The psychological aspect is also at stake: the bus is slower, exposes commuters to road traffic, introduces variability. A 24-30 hour railway interruption generates stress among cross-border commuters, especially if they have no plan B. Those who have access to a private car might consider driving through border crossings, but this introduces additional fuel costs. Those entirely dependent on public transport have no choice but to adapt to the replacement buses and accept the inevitable delays.
### What changes in daily travel management
The official recommendation to 'inform yourself shortly before departure' is not a mere suggestion. It means contacting railway operators, consulting mobility apps (SBB Mobil, Trenord), checking for updates on delays or cancellations. A positive development in repairs could accelerate restoration; a negative development could prolong the interruption. Between 30-60 minutes before departure, it is essential to have the most current information, because the situation can change rapidly.
For employers who hire cross-border commuters, this period represents a management challenge: documented delays cannot be charged to workers, but still create organizational problems. For cross-border commuters themselves, the risk is concrete: one or two days of small delays could go unnoticed, but the message sent to the employer (even if unfair) is unreliability. The psychological pressure is real.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## How to Organize During the Interruption
If you regularly travel on the Cadenazzo–Luino route for work, consider these concrete steps in the coming two days:
**Contact your employer**: Report the railway service interruption before the morning. Many employers, especially in Lombardy, understand cross-border service disruptions and can allow a delayed departure or authorize exceptional remote work for that day.
Check official bus schedules: SBB Mobil, Trenord and local bus operators will provide updated schedules. Don't rely on third-hand information or social media. Official apps are the source of truth.
Add buffer time: If your normal journey takes 45 minutes by train, expect 90 minutes by bus. Leave 30-45 minutes earlier than you normally would. This safety margin protects you from surprises.
Consider alternative transport: If you have access to a private car and fuel costs are manageable, consider a private ride or carpooling with other cross-border workers in the same situation. Ask in Ticino cross-border worker WhatsApp groups if anyone is organizing a ride to the Luino area.
### Timeline and Deadlines
The interruption continues until Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 4:00 AM. This means that Tuesday, September 8 (today) the service is blocked, and will remain so for the entire day and the following night. Starting at 4:00 AM on Wednesday morning, normal railway traffic on the route is expected to resume. If you work night shifts or are returning very late Tuesday evening, check if there are replacement buses in the evening hours as well, since some routes may be reduced or cancelled during the night.
### Resources and Support Links
To organize yourself best, consult the [border crossing guide](nav:border) if you are considering road alternatives, and learn how to plan the costs of your daily commute as a cross-border worker. Stay updated by frequently checking official channels until complete restoration. Share reliable information with fellow cross-border workers — the informal support network is precious in these critical moments.
First day as a cross-border worker? Our [practical guide](nav:first-day) walks you from cantonal registration to your first paycheck.

item.title: Swiss cross-border commuters: 400,000, myths and analysis
item.description: Switzerland employs 400,000+ border workers (European record). New book dispels myths: growth 1978–2026, wages, taxation, transport. Ticino in the centre.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Switzerland employs 400,000+ cross-border workers: European record in 2026 - From 1978 to today: growth from 84,000 to over 400,000 (+376%) - New book analyzes myths, salaries, taxation and cross-border transport - Ticino, French-speaking Switzerland and Basel absorb 80% of the workforce
## Key Facts - **What**: Book 'Le travail frontalier en Suisse - 30 questions' debunks myths and analyzes the phenomenon - When: Published in 2026 (data from 1978 to today) - Where: Three main areas: French-speaking Switzerland, Ticino, Basel - Who: Authors: Stéphane Rossini (former director of FSIO), Jean-Claude Rennwald (former union leader), Daniel Droz (journalist), Alexandre Moine (geographer) - Amount: 84,000 cross-border workers in 1978 → 400,000+ in 2026 - Publisher: Alphil - Agreement: Free movement Switzerland-EU since 2000
Switzerland has achieved an unprecedented milestone in Europe: it employs over 400,000 cross-border workers. To understand what this means in concrete terms, one need only look at the past. In 1978, following the economic crisis of 1974-75, there were only 84,000 cross-border workers. The leap in time — from just under 100,000 to four times as many — was not linear, but experienced a decisive acceleration after 2000, when the agreement on the free movement of persons between Switzerland and the European Union came into force. The robustness of the Swiss economy did the rest.
A new book titled 'Le travail frontalier en Suisse - 30 questions' (Alphil) addresses this reality with data in hand. The authors are four: the former socialist national councillors Stéphane Rossini (Valais, former director of the Federal Office of Social Insurance) and Jean-Claude Rennwald (Jura, union leader), supported by journalist Daniel Droz and geographer Alexandre Moine. The work focuses on three geographic areas that alone absorb over 80% of the cross-border workforce: French-speaking Switzerland, Ticino and the two cantons of Basel.
### From Numbers to Myths
The themes addressed by the book are multiple: employment, wages, social dumping, social security, taxation, training, housing, territorial planning and transport. But there is a question that recurs frequently in public debates: do cross-border workers really steal jobs from resident workers? For Rennwald, xenophobic reflexes towards cross-border workers seem less pronounced today compared to a few decades ago. They could, however, ease further if the use of public transport were to increase. Traffic on roads and highways, with its eternal congestion, remains indeed one of the main sources of friction between communities. ### Structural growth in 48 years
From 1978 to 2026, the number of cross-border workers in Switzerland has grown nearly 4.8 times. It is not a random growth, nor is it a consequence of massive immigration. Rather, it is the structural result of two factors: the economic integration that followed the free movement agreement of 2000, and the persistent development disparity between European economies. Switzerland, with its salaries and the quality of work, remains a powerful pole of attraction for those living on the other side of the border — especially in Ticino, where the borders with Italy allow a daily commute that is not always easy, but feasible.
The three areas that absorb over 80% of the cross-border workforce have diverse characteristics. French-speaking Switzerland (Vaud, Jura, Valais, Geneva) attracts mainly from border regions in France. Ticino, especially with the Mendrisio district, engages with Lombard provinces. The two Basel cantons (BS and BL) receive workers from Alsace, central France, and southwestern Germany. Each area has developed a cross-border economy with its own peculiarities and specific labor market dynamics.
### The myth of the 'theft of jobs'
The question of whether cross-border workers 'steal jobs from residents' is complex. The book does not provide a simplistic answer. According to the authors, cross-border work is the result of globalization and unequal development in the capitalist system. For this reason, say Rossini and Rennwald, it will be possible to regulate it only through the construction of a social Switzerland and a social Europe — that is, through greater harmonization of salaries, labor rights, and social protection between countries.
Wage dumping, differentiated taxation, and the lack of equal protections remain critical points. However, the authors note that xenophobic reactions toward cross-border workers are today less pronounced than they were a few decades ago. One of the causes of this change is the growing acceptance that the phenomenon is not reversible — it is a structural characteristic of contemporary Europe, not a temporary exception.
### The role of transportation in public opinion
An interesting discovery from the book: traffic and congestion at Alpine passes remain one of the strongest sources of friction between Swiss residents and cross-border workers. It is not directly a matter of employment, but of daily livability. The more cross-border workers use public transport — buses, trains, organized shuttles — the less visibility congestion at highways has. Paradoxically, better public transportation infrastructure could reduce tensions more than any awareness campaign, making commuting less perceptible to the local community.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What it means concretely for the cross-border worker
If you work daily across the border, the content of this book concerns you directly. It is not an abstract treatise on economic sociology, but a manual that answers 30 concrete questions about the aspects that affect your life: salaries, taxes, permits, social security, housing and mobility.
The growth from 84,000 to 400,000 cross-border workers in 48 years means that your status is no longer considered an anomaly, but a permanent reality of the Swiss economy. This has positive implications (greater regulatory recognition, more stable bilateral agreements) and persistent challenges (wage competition in low-skilled sectors, fiscal complexity in double taxation). The book analyzes how these phenomena manifest in the three main areas — including Ticino — and what role public policies play in regulating them.
### Where to deepen and which tools to use
For those wishing to read the complete book, «Le travail frontalier en Suisse - 30 questions» is available from the publisher Alphil and in major Swiss bookstores. If instead you are interested in understanding the specific fiscal and salary impacts of your situation, the Frontaliere Ticino website provides [a net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and [tax return tools](nav:tax-return) that allow you to concretely see how the various components of your income are composed month by month.
Furthermore, if you wish to explore additional [job offers in Switzerland](nav:jobs) in light of these analyses, you can consult the dedicated section. The book provides the general framework; our tools help you navigate daily practice, transforming theory into real numbers of your payslip.

item.description: According to bonus.ch, LAMal premiums will increase by almost 5% in 2027, with peaks of up to 20%. Direct impact on border workers' paychecks.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Health insurance premiums will increase by nearly 5% in 2027 compared to 2026 - In 2026, the increase was 4.4% - Some policyholders will face increases of up to 20% - The Confederation will communicate the official data by the end of the month
## Key facts - **Average increase**: nearly 5% (scenario 4.5%-5%) - Previous year: 4.4% in 2026 - Maximum peaks: up to 20% for some policyholders - Source of forecast: bonus.ch (online comparison tool) - Official data: by the end of September from the Confederation - Sector: Compulsory health insurance (LAMal) - Period: In effect January 1, 2027
A new, significant increase in health insurance premiums is looming for 2027. According to the online comparison tool bonus.ch, the average increase will be nearly 5%, higher than the 4.4% recorded in 2026. Those warning of this continued upward trend are the authors of the survey on the comparison portal themselves, who comment: 'The hope for a truce seems to be slipping away once again.'
The most worrying figures, however, concern those in specific situations: some policyholders will even have to deal with peaks of up to 20%. This is not an unexpected phenomenon, but a reality already highlighted by online comparison tools that collect preventive data from health insurance funds in anticipation of the new year.
### Direct impact on cross-border workers For those working in Switzerland with a G permit—a category that includes the majority of Italian cross-border workers—the increase in LAMal premiums is a direct cost on the monthly paycheck. It is not a tax, but an individual insurance burden deducted from the salary. When bonus.ch reports increases of 5%, this translates into a concrete price increase that reduces the net monthly income of each cross-border worker, regardless of income.
### Awaiting official data To have definitive figures, we must wait for the official communication from the Confederation, expected by the end of September 2026. However, the trend is already clear: bonus.ch estimates a plausible scenario of between 4.5% and 5%, taking into account the trend in compulsory health insurance costs (AOMS), the financial situation of health insurance funds, and the slight recovery effect expected.
### No respite in sight The most relevant figure for those managing a cross-border family budget is this: economic pressure will not ease even in 2027. Previous years have already seen steady increases, and 2027 does not seem to offer any relief. The premium system continues to grow beyond official inflation, eroding year after year the purchasing power of workers.
### What to monitor In the Canton Ticino, where Italian cross-border workers represent a significant share of the workforce, this increase directly affects thousands of monthly paychecks. Until the official communication from the Confederation, it is advisable to monitor the first communications from individual health insurance funds, which will begin notifying 2027 premiums in October-November. For more information on available coverage, consult our dedicated section [nav:health]. ## How the increase impacts the border family budget
The nearly 5% increase may not seem dramatic until you apply it to concrete figures. A border worker with a G permit who pays a LAMal premium of CHF 400 per month — a realistic figure for an adult with an average deductible — will see the amount rise to around CHF 420 per month in 2027. On an annual basis, it means about CHF 240 more.
For those who have a family (spouse + 1-2 children), the multiplier is even more pronounced. If the core pays CHF 1,000 total monthly, the 5% increase leads to CHF 50 more each month, or CHF 600 per year. These figures are not insignificant for those who already manage the gap between the cost of living in Ticino and the Swiss salary.
### Comparison with 2026 and historical trend The 2026 increase had been 4.4%. The change from 4.4% to almost-5% represents an acceleration, albeit modest numerically. What matters is the trend: in recent years, premiums have never registered significant declines, and increases are constantly between 3% and 5% per year. This means that the cost of sick pay grows faster than wages for most workers.
### Strategies to contain damage: cash changeover The first lever available to the border agent is the cash changeover. All policyholders — with a G or B permit — have the right to choose a different cashier each year, with effect from 1 January of the following year.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Step-by-step procedure for adapting to the premium increase
Addressing the increase in LAMal premiums in 2027 requires a series of concrete actions, articulated on a precise timeline. Here's what to do and when.
### Step 1: Wait for official Confederation data (by end of September 2026) The first action is passive: wait for the official communication from the Confederation, expected by the end of September 2026. It is not wise to speculate on preliminary estimates or national averages. Official data will provide the certified increase for each canton. Until then, bonus.ch estimates (4.5%-5%) remain the most reliable, but are not definitive.
### Step 2: Collect communications from health insurance funds (October-November 2026) Between mid-October and the end of November, each health insurance fund will notify its policyholders of the new premium amount effective January 1, 2027. This communication usually arrives by ordinary mail or through access to the personal area on the insurance company's website. Do not be surprised by this communication: it is expected and foreseeable.
### Step 3: Compare alternatives on bonus.ch (by November 2026) Upon receipt of the new premium notification, open the online bonus.ch comparator and enter your data (age, postal code, desired type of coverage). The portal will show all premiums available from different health insurance funds for 2027. Often it turns out that a competing fund offers a significantly lower premium. The annual difference can exceed CHF 200-300 in some cases.
### Step 4: Decide whether to change insurance provider (by November 2026) If the comparison reveals a more convenient health insurance fund, make the decision to switch before the deadline of November 30, 2026. The change is free and involves no penalties or administrative costs. The only thing to do is fill out the cancellation form with your current fund and the registration form with the new fund.
### Step 5: Simulate the impact on your 2027 payslip (December 2026) Use our online calculator [nav:payslip] to simulate how the new LAMal premium will affect your monthly net salary in 2027. Enter the new premium amount, gross salary, and other tax data, and the calculator will show the net amount. This allows you to plan your household budget with precision.
### Step 6: Communicate with your employer (if necessary) If the change of insurance provider involves a significant variation in the premium, communicate it to your employer (if operating in Switzerland) so they can update your payslip from January 2027. If the cross-border worker also receives salary from Italy (remote work, dual contract), check with the tax consultant how to reflect the change in taxes.
## Tools to optimize your choice
### Payslip Calculator Use our calculator [nav:payslip] to update in real time how the new LAMal premium and Swiss contributions will affect your 2027 net salary. Enter your gross salary, the cantonal tax rate (Ticino or other), and the new LAMal premium, and you will get a precise estimate.
### Currency Exchange Comparator If you work in Switzerland but spend euros in Italy, the CHF/EUR exchange rate impacts your purchasing power. Check our comparator [nav:exchange] to monitor the exchange rate in the coming months.
### LAMal Information For specific questions about insurance coverage, available deductibles, or cross-border worker rights, consult our dedicated health insurance section [nav:health].
## Conclusion: act now to save in 2027
The almost 5% increase in LAMal premiums in 2027 is not a surprise, but a known consequence of the structure of Swiss healthcare costs. However, the cross-border worker is not passive in the face of this price increase: they have the power to choose the most convenient health insurance fund and to plan their budget in advance.
By acting by November 2026 — verifying new premiums, comparing alternatives, and calculating the payslip impact — it is possible to minimize the damage and, in some cases, save hundreds of francs per year. The key is timely information and conscious action.

item.description: bonus.ch forecasts an average increase of almost 5% by 2027, up from 4.4% in 2026. Some policyholders face spikes of up to 20%. Ticino practically stable.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Average premium increase 2027: approximately 5% (higher than 4.4% in 2026) - Some policyholders face peaks up to 20% - Confederation will communicate official figures end of month - Ticino relatively stable: -0.1% in 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Increase in mandatory Swiss health insurance premiums (LAMal/CMI) - When: 2027, announcement end of September 2026 - Where: All of Switzerland; Ticino -0.1% in 2026 - Who: bonus.ch and Keystone-ATS - Average increase: 4.5%-5% (most plausible scenario) - Maximum peaks: up to 20% in specific cases
The increase in health insurance premiums that will hit Swiss policyholders in 2027 will be even heavier than that in 2026. According to the online comparison tool bonus.ch, the average increase will amount to nearly 5%, higher than the 4.4% recorded this year. It is not good news for those working in Switzerland, from employees to Ticino-Italy cross-border workers who pay their LAMal contributions every month.
The bonus.ch survey, reported by Keystone-ATS, was presented today and casts an even longer shadow over the situation of personal finances. The authors comment that 'hope for a respite seems to be slipping away once more'. To get the official data, however, we will have to wait until the end of September, when the Confederation will communicate the final figures.
### Three possible scenarios
The bonus.ch analysis outlines three plausible scenarios. The most likely scenario is an average increase of 4.5%-5%, which analysts consider the most realistic taking into account the trend in mandatory insurance costs (AOMS), the financial situation of health insurance funds, and the slight recovery effect expected. A favorable scenario would bring the increase to 3.5%-4%, but would require a sharper slowdown in costs than that predicted by current models. Conversely, an unfavorable scenario could exceed the 5% threshold if 2026 expenses exceeded estimates or if the transition to new ambulatory tariffs entailed unforeseen additional costs.
However, the national average masks strong disparities at the personal level. Some policyholders face peaks up to 20%, while others will see more modest increases. It all depends on the chosen health insurance fund, the canton of residence, the tariff zone, age, the deductible, and the chosen model. ### Regional variations: Canton Ticino in a relative advantage
Regional variations are particularly relevant for the cross-border worker who works in a specific canton and pays [LAMal](nav:health) contributions monthly. In the second quarter of 2026, healthcare cost trends showed marked differences: while the Swiss average stood at +0.4%, Canton Schaffhausen registered +9.6% and Zug even -8.7%. In between, the Grisons position themselves at +3.7%, while **Canton Ticino** — the most relevant for the Italy-Switzerland cross-border worker — is practically stable at -0.1%. This represents a small glimmer of hope: those who work and are insured in the canton will not face particularly heavy increases compared to other Swiss regions.
But not all insured persons will see the same increase. Beyond the canton, the specific health insurance fund chosen, the local tariff zone, the insured person's age, the deductible level, and the selected coverage model (HMO, PPP, traditional insurance) all have an impact. Some companies or tariff categories will register increases of more than 10%; in the most unfortunate cases, even over 20%.
### Which services cost more: the impact on care
The increase is not uniform across healthcare services. Some categories are hit harder: home care approximately 15%, psychologists and psychotherapists 10%, physiotherapists 7%, outpatient physicians 6%. For the cross-border worker who frequently needs these services — weekly psychological visits, physiotherapy sessions after an injury, home care for an elderly parent — the impact on the deductible reached and on the cost-sharing (participant participation) could be significant. The total cost of care will rise more than the general average.
### Effect on the paycheck
For the cross-border worker, LAMal contributions are deducted from gross salary before the calculation of federal and cantonal taxes. A 5% increase in premiums means directly less net CHF in the pocket each month. If a cross-border worker currently pays CHF 300 per month for health insurance, a 5% increase equals CHF 15 less per month, approximately CHF 180 per year. For those with a family, with multiple insured persons (spouse, children), the impact multiplies rapidly.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to compare premiums and when to act
August and September are the critical months for those who want to save on premiums: this is when health insurance funds communicate increases and when insured individuals still have time to change coverage. At the end of September 2026 (usual date), the Confederation will officially announce the new cantonal premiums for 2027.
The cross-border worker should follow these steps:
1. Wait for the official Confederation announcement: end of September 2026 is the key date for definitive data 2. Verify your health insurance fund's letter: it will arrive in the following days with the new premium and variations 3. Compare online: bonus.ch and other comparison tools allow you to see all available alternatives in your canton and tariff zone 4. Evaluate changing insurance fund or plan model: you can change until 30 November 2026 to have effect from 1 January 2027 5. Check the deductible: choosing a higher deductible (CHF 500 instead of CHF 300) reduces the monthly premium but increases out-of-pocket expenses when care is needed
### Deadlines and documents
- Official premium announcement: end of September 2026 (from the Confederation) - Health insurance fund letter: by October 2026 with the new premium - Deadline for change: 30 November 2026 (the change takes effect from 1 January 2027) - Verification with CMI: cross-border workers with Permit G can check whether they fall into the categories that can opt for Italian insurance instead of Swiss insurance
For the cross-border worker who wants to understand the exact impact on their 2027 take-home pay, it is useful to [calculate the new net](nav:calculator) with the increased LAMal contribution, so you can realistically plan your monthly budget. If changing health insurance funds seems convenient, it is best to act before the November deadline. Also check the portability clauses of your current policy and the benefits covered in the alternative plan before deciding.
### Don't be caught off guard
Not everyone knows that the right to change exists and is free. If your current insurance fund's new offer is unacceptable, other companies might offer better conditions in the same canton or tariff zone. Consulting [the most convenient health insurance](nav:health) allows you not to passively suffer a 20% increase when perhaps the average in Canton Ticino or in the area where you work is lower. The window is short (September-November 2026): it's better to act in good time.

The choice to pursue a university education in the Canton of Ticino by enrolling at the Università della Svizzera italiana (USI) or the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI) represents an important step for many young people residing in Italy. Unlike those who cross border checkpoints such as Brogeda or Gaggiolo daily for professional reasons, the commuting student operates within a profoundly different regulatory and administrative framework, which does not provide the same tax or social security rules applied to employees subject to withholding tax or registered with social security institutions.
### Academic commuting dynamics Daily or weekly travel between the Italian border provinces and Ticino's university hubs requires careful logistical organization. The road and rail routes connecting Lombardy to the Canton of Ticino are crossed daily by thousands of people, but the concessions reserved for workers with a G permit do not automatically apply to students. The latter must in fact deal with regulations relating to study residence permits issued by the competent authorities, such as the Population Section of the Canton of Ticino, which regulate stay on Swiss territory for educational purposes.
Financial planning for a university course of study in Switzerland also requires a precise evaluation of out-of-pocket expenses, which include academic fees, cross-border public transport costs, and any accommodation expenses for those who choose to reside temporarily near the campuses of Lugano, Mendrizzi, or Bellinzona. Unlike cross-border workers, who benefit from specific regimes linked to the new tax agreement and related exemptions, students must rely on family resources or any scholarships made available through institutional calls for applications. ### Key differences with cross-border commuting It is essential to draw a clear line of demarcation between the condition of the university commuter student and that of the traditional cross-border worker. While the latter earns employment income subject to taxation according to the criteria established by the double taxation convention and the new agreement signed between Italy and Switzerland, the student does not produce a main professional income deriving from an occupation subject to ordinary withholding tax.
### Logistic and residential aspects Those who choose to commute between Italy and Ticino to attend classes at USI or SUPSI must evaluate whether to maintain their registered residence in Italy or apply for a student residence permit in Switzerland. This choice directly affects access to healthcare services, mandatory insurance coverage, and the management of identity and transit documents. If the student decides to temporarily relocate to Ticino, specific obligations arise related to the notification of arrival at the Ticino municipality of domicile and the taking out of insurance policies complying with Swiss standards.
### Economic planning and ancillary expenses Living costs in Canton Ticino are notoriously higher than those in bordering Italian regions. For a commuting student, this gap is reflected not only in dining expenses and study materials, but also in the purchase of passes for local and regional public transport. Careful management of the monthly budget must take into account fluctuations in the exchange rate between the Euro and the Swiss Franc, a factor that impacts the purchasing power of those who receive funds in European currency but incur current expenses in CHF.

First of all, it is necessary to check with the student secretariats of USI or SUPSI the list of documents required for admission and for the issuance of the documentation useful for obtaining the residence permit for study purposes at the competent cantonal offices. item.title: G Bewilligung Antrag 2026: documents and procedure for cross-border commuters
item.description: Permit G in Canton Ticino: documents, procedure at the Migrationsamt, five-year validity and renewal after the New Frontier Agreement 2024.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit G: residence permit for Italian border workers in Canton Ticino - Validity 5 years from the date of issue, with the possibility of renewal - New Frontier Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 - Tax at source withheld only in Switzerland, tax credit in Italy
## Key facts - **What**: G (Grenzgängerbewilligung) permit for frontier workers - When: Application submitted before the start of business in Switzerland - Where: Migration Office of the Canton of Ticino (Migrationsamt) and Municipality of Italian residence - Who: Swiss employer (forwarding), frontier worker (signature and documents) - Validity: 5 years from date of issue, renewable - Reference: New Agreement signed 23/12/2020, in force from 1 January 2024 - Italian ratification: Law 83 of 13 June 2023 - Double taxation agreement: signed on 9 December 1976
An Italian border worker who starts a subordinate activity in Canton Ticino must obtain the G permit before crossing the border daily to go to work. The procedure is governed by the federal law on foreigners and by Ticino cantonal practice, with the New Italian-Swiss Frontier Agreement — signed on 23 December 2020 and in force from 1 January 2024 after Italian ratification with Law 83 of 13 June 2023 — which redesigned the tax and contribution perimeter of workers at the border.
### Who initiates the procedure The Swiss employer The G permit is neither a tourist visa nor a residence permit: it is a specific authorisation for those who maintain their domicile in Italy — typically in the provinces of Como, Varese, Lecco, Monza-Brianza, Bergamo or Sondrio — and return daily to Ticino for work. This characteristic determines the entire tax and social security treatment of the worker.
### Source taxation, not double taxation From 1 January 2024, the New Cross-Border Workers Agreement introduced a tax-free allowance of €10,000 for new cross-border workers, while workers already employed before 17 July 2023 benefit from a €7,500 exemption and a transitional regime that phases in the tax burden until 2033. Source tax is withheld exclusively in Switzerland: Italy avoids double taxation through the tax credit mechanism, to be indicated in section CE of the 730 form.
This framework also applies to social security contributions: OASI/DI/IC (5.3% borne by the employee), unemployment insurance UI/LA (1.1% up to a maximum of CHF 148,200 in salary), LAAI (between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on sectoral risk) and LPP (from 7% to 18% by age bracket, starting from age 25) are withheld at source in Switzerland. For supplementary pension benefits, compare the contributions with the [payslip simulator](nav:payslip) to estimate the impact on net income.
### Old and new cross-border workers: two regimes compared The distinction between 'old cross-border worker' and 'new cross-border worker' is not a bureaucratic detail: it determines the size of the tax-free allowance, the transition schedule and the scope of applicable collective agreements. When renewing the G permit every five years, it is advisable to check with the employer and a tax advisor that the applied regime is consistent with the date of hire. For an updated comparison between the two categories, use the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) which reproduces the Italian IRPEF brackets (23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001 and €50,000, 43% above €50,000) applied to the tax credit.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). Obtaining the G permit in 2026 means submitting an application that is orderly, complete, and consistent with the practice of the Ticino Migrationsamt. The procedure can be broken down into five operational steps, each with specific deadlines and documents.
### Step 1 — Verification of Requirements Before Applying Before sending any documents, the cross-border candidate must confirm that they are an Italian citizen (or a citizen of another EU/EFTA State), have no criminal record incompatible with admission to Switzerland, and have signed an employment contract with an employer based in Canton Ticino. The registered residence must remain in Italy, in a Municipality reachable from a border crossing — Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, or Ponte Tresa — with daily return.
### Step 2 — Document Collection The documentation normally required includes: a valid passport or identity card, a historical residence certificate, a criminal record extract, a civil status certificate (for married applicants and dependent children), the employment contract signed by the Swiss employer, and a description of the role. For non-EU workers, an Italian residence permit and proof of entry visa must also be added. Italian documents must be translated by a sworn translator if required by the SEM.
### Step 3 — Submission of the Application by the Employer The Swiss employer submits the application through the cantonal portal or directly at the Migrationsamt desk in Bellinzona. The file contains the official form, a copy of the contract, and the candidate's attachments. From that moment, the Canton begins its investigation: it verifies the existence of the position, the contribution coverage, and compatibility with the priority given to resident workers.
### Step 4 — Permit Receipt and Registration Once the application is approved, the cross-border worker receives the G permit in paper format or as an electronic card. They must carry it at the border crossing during the first transits and provide a copy to their Italian Municipality of residence for population register updates. The permit is valid for five years; upon expiry, renewal follows the same procedure, unless there are changes in the employment relationship (change of employer, modification of the percentage, promotion to a managerial role).
### Step 5 — Tax and Contribution Obligations With the permit in hand, the cross-border worker is automatically enrolled in Swiss AVS/AI/IPG, in the LPP pension fund indicated by the employer, and, unless opting out, in Swiss LAMal — with the right to choose health insurance and an annual deductible regulated by federal law between CHF 300 and CHF 2'500 for adults. Withholding tax is calculated on the Swiss salary according to Ticino cantonal rates, administered at the federal level by the AFC/ESTV. To estimate the net amount and contributions, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) updated for 2026.

### The regulatory framework Currenly, the Double Taxation Convention between Italy and Switzerland was signed on December 9, 1976. Subsequently, the New Agreement for cross-border workers was signed on December 23, 2020 and officially entered into force on January 1, 2024, with Italian ratification taking place via Law 83 of June 13, 2023. This regulatory evolution has redefined the tax perimeter for thousands of workers who cross border checkpoints such as Brogeda every day to go to the Canton of Ticino, clearly distinguishing between the position of those who started before or after the watershed date of July 17, 2023.

An employee hired in the Canton of Ticino with a gross annual income of 60,000 Swiss francs who falls under the category of new cross-border workers benefits from the 10,000 euro exemption provided by Italian regulations. The withholding tax applied by the Swiss authorities is declared in Italy using the 730 model, entering the data in section CE to obtain the tax credit and avoid double taxation. Workers active in border municipalities such as Mendrisio or Chiasso must annually verify the certifications issued by their Swiss employer to complete their tax return by the Italian tax deadlines. ## In short
 - Three nights of closure on the A8 Milan-Varese motorway towards Varese
 - Work on noise barriers from September 9 to 11, 2026
 - Closing times: 9:00 PM - 5:00 AM
 - Cavaria and Solbiate Arno junctions closed for entry

 ## Key Facts
 - **What**: Night closure of the A8 section and junctions for noise barrier works
 - When: Wednesday 9th, Thursday 10th, and Friday 11th September 2026, 9:00 PM - 5:00 AM
 - Where: A8 Milan-Varese, section between the D08 Gallarate-Gattico branch and Castronno, towards Varese
 - Who: motorway operators (not specified in the source)
 - Amount: not specified
 - Closed section: from Gallarate-Gattico branch to Castronno, towards Varese
 - Closed junctions: Cavaria and Solbiate Arno inbound, both directions
 - Vehicles involved: light vehicles under 3.5 tons and heavy vehicles over 3.5 tons (different routes)

 Another round of nighttime closures on the A8 Milan-Varese motorway due to noise barrier upgrades. Restrictions are in place for the three nights of Wednesday, September 9th, Thursday, September 10th, and Friday, September 11th, 2026, from 9:00 PM to 5:00 AM, in the Varese direction.

 ### Closed section and affected junctions

 The section between the junction with the D08 Gallarate-Gattico branch and Castronno, in the direction of Varese, will be closed. The Cavaria and Solbiate Arno junctions will be closed for entry in both directions, Varese and Milan. At the same time, the D08 branch will be closed. The work on the noise barriers along the A8 Milan-Varese motorway affects one of the busiest arteries used by commuters who return every evening from the Milan direction towards Varese and the upper Varese area. The decision to concentrate the works during nighttime hours, between 9:00 PM and 5:00 AM, aims to limit the impact on commuter traffic, but it does not eliminate the inconvenience for those travelling in that time slot, such as truck drivers, evening shift workers, and cross-border commuters returning late.
### Why these closures matter for local mobility
The A8 Milan-Varese is not just an internal Lombardy motorway section: it is the direct connection between the Varese network and the A8/A9 that continues towards the Swiss border. Vehicles coming from the Gallarate-Gattico spur (D08) and from the A26 Genova Voltri-Gravellona Toce, heading towards Varese, will find the entry ramp towards Varese closed for three nights. Those who travel this stretch daily know that the mandatory detours onto the ordinary road network — SP49, SP26, SS341 — extend travel times by twenty to thirty minutes during the evening rush hours.
The differentiation of routes between light and heavy vehicles is not a technical detail: it reflects a physical constraint, the Albizzate underpass which cannot be used by vehicles over 3.5 tonnes, which forces trucks onto a more complex route, passing through via De Gasperi, via Carabelli, and via XXV Aprile, urban streets that require greater attention and longer travel times.
### "What if" scenario
A commuter returning from Milan after 9:00 PM towards Castronno or Albizzate will find the Cavaria entry slip road closed: they will have to continue to Gallarate and re-enter from the SS341. Those coming from the A26 towards Varese will find the entry ramp closed on the D08 and will have to exit at Besnate, dealing with the ordinary road network. For heavy vehicles the route will be even more complex, with a transit ban under the Albizzate underpass.
The closures of the Cavaria and Solbiate Arno entry slip roads in both directions mean that even those who only need to enter the motorway will not be able to do so from those toll booths: for those heading towards Varese, Castronno is recommended; for those heading towards Milan, Gallarate is recommended; for those who need to take the D08 Gallarate-Gattico spur, Besnate is recommended.
For those who regularly travel this stretch, it is useful to check in advance the waiting times at the border crossings, because any queues on the A8 can spill over onto the ordinary road network that leads towards the Varese network.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). For those traveling on the A8 Milan-Varese motorway during the nights between Wednesday 9 and Friday 11 September 2026, here is what to do concretely.
### Procedure for light vehicles (under 3.5 tonnes)
Step 1: identify your point of origin. Those coming from the A8 towards Varese who have already passed the Gallarate exit must continue mandatorily onto the D08 Gallarate-Gattico spur, exiting at Besnate at km 4+000.
Step 2: travel on ordinary roads: SP49, SP26 towards Jerago con Orago/Solbiate Arno, SS341 towards Albizzate/Castronno.
Step 3: re-enter the A8 at the Castronno junction, towards Varese.
Those who exit earlier at Gallarate must instead follow the SP341 towards Cavaria/Solbiate Arno/Albizzate/Castronno and re-enter at Castronno.
### Procedure for heavy vehicles (over 3.5 tonnes)
Step 1: due to the underpass in the municipality of Albizzate being impassable, heavy vehicles must follow the alternative route even when they would already be on the light-vehicle path.
Step 2: exit at Gallarate (or at Besnate if Gallarate has already been passed), travel along SS341 towards Cavaria/Solbiate Arno/Albizzate, via De Gasperi, via Carabelli, via XXV Aprile, SS341 towards Castronno.
Step 3: re-enter the A8 at the Castronno junction.
### Closures of the Cavaria and Solbiate Arno junctions
For those who need to enter the motorway from Cavaria or Solbiate Arno: - towards Varese: use the Castronno junction on the same A8; - towards Milan: use the Gallarate junction on the same A8; - towards the D08 Gallarate-Gattico spur: use the Besnate junction on the D08.
### Closure of the D08/A8 branch towards Varese
For those coming from the A26 Genova Voltri-Gravellona Toce and traveling on the D08 Gallarate-Gattico spur, with destination Varese: exit in advance at the Besnate station, travel along SP49, SP26 towards Jerago con Orago/Solbiate Arno (or Albizzate for heavy vehicles), SS341 towards Castronno and enter the A8 at the Castronno junction towards Varese. Those who pass Besnate must continue mandatorily on the A8 towards Milan, exit at Gallarate, travel along SS341 to Castronno and re-enter the A8 towards Varese.
To best plan your movements during these nights of works, it is useful to [use the net salary calculator](nav:calculator) to assess the impact of any evening shifts on your net pay, or to [consult the border crossings map](nav:border-map) for those continuing beyond Varese towards Switzerland.

The new border agreement, signed on December 23, 2020, has been in effect since January 1, 2024. This agreement introduced a franchise of €10,000 for new border workers, replacing the previous exemption of €7,500 for old border workers. The franchise is valid for work-related income and is only applied in Switzerland, avoiding double taxation with Italy through the 730 CE tax credit.
### Advantages of the new agreement The new agreement offers several advantages to border workers. The higher franchise of €10,000 provides greater tax protection, while the transitional regime for old border workers until 2033 ensures a smoother transition. Additionally, the agreement establishes that the withholding tax is only withheld in Switzerland, simplifying the tax management for border workers.
### Disadvantages of the new agreement Despite the advantages, the new agreement also presents some disadvantages. The franchise of €10,000 is lower than that provided by the old agreement, which amounted to €7,500. Additionally, the new agreement does not include a franchise for non-work-related income, such as bank interest or rental income.

A border worker living in Nus and working in Vaud, with an annual income of €30,000, will have a franchise of €10,000 applied to their Swiss income. This means that only €20,000 of the income will be taxed in Switzerland, at a rate of 13.8% (2024), resulting in a tax of €2,760. If the border worker had been covered by the old agreement, they would have had a franchise of €7,500, reducing the tax to €2,130. However, with the new agreement, the franchise is higher, offering greater tax protection.

The Varese Chamber of Commerce is promoting a meeting dedicated to Renewable Energy Communities, the so-called CER, designed to illustrate how businesses, local authorities, and private citizens can produce, consume, and share clean energy in the territory. The event arises from the collaboration between the Varese Chamber of Commerce and the Malpensa Insubria CER Association, with the declared objective of transforming environmental sustainability into a concrete resource for the economic and social system of the territory.
### An initiative to reduce the impact of energy costs The initiative aims to provide practical answers to those who intend to reduce the impact of energy costs through the use of renewable sources. According to the Chamber of Commerce, being part of a CER allows access to more efficient resource management, increasing the competitiveness of small and medium-sized enterprises and improving the sustainability of public services offered by local authorities.
During the event, key aspects related to energy security and flexibility will be analyzed. Among the central themes is self-sufficiency, a factor that — according to the source — is fundamental to protecting businesses and families from price fluctuations generated by the international geopolitical context.
### Sharing and new Chamber of Commerce tender Joining a Renewable Energy Community means, in the words of the Varese Chamber of Commerce, overcoming the traditional consumption model to embrace a network logic. Sharing the energy produced in the territory allows the generation of a widespread value, to the benefit of both the environment and the local economy.
During the conference, the new tender promoted by the Varese Chamber of Commerce will also be officially presented. The measure aims to economically support the realization of photovoltaic plants intended for entry into CER, offering direct financial aid to those who choose to invest in solar energy. For workers who cross the border daily — from Ponte Tresa to Chiasso, from Brogeda to Gaggiolo — household energy expenses represent a significant portion of the monthly budget, especially during periods of tariff increases. La costruzione della Rete Tram-Treno sta per iniziare. Lunedì mattina davanti alla stampa è stato annunciato che nella seconda metà di ottobre si comincerà con i muri di controriva sulla tratta Bioggio-Manno. Nei primi mesi dell’anno prossimo toccherà al pozzo di collegamento alla stazione ferroviaria a Besso e al portale lato ovest della galleria di Breganzona alla Crespera.
In pratica è la prima parte del progetto: una galleria di oltre due chilometri che collega con il centro città di Lugano. I cantieri non sono invisibili e quindi la popolazione sarà informata, ha assicurato Alberto Del Col, direttore della società Rete Tram Treno.
«Con cantieri di queste dimensioni – ha dichiarato al Radiogiornale della RSI - è fondamentale continuare a tenere curato quello che è il rapporto con tutti i coinvolti sia contrattualmente sia le autorità, ma poi anche e soprattutto la popolazione, perché la popolazione, se è vero che un domani avrà i vantaggi che porta un progetto di questo tipo, è anche vero che nel corso dei cantieri, chi più chi meno, si accorgerà di quello che succede e quindi è giusto che sia informata e giusto che sappia quali sono le misure che mettiamo in atto per restare entro i parametri di legge».
### Impatto sui frontalieri
I lavori per la Rete Tram-Treno avranno un impatto significativo sulla vita quotidiana dei frontalieri che utilizzano questa tratta per spostarsi tra Italia e Svizzera. La società Rete Tram Treno ha assicurato che verranno messe in atto misure per limitare i disagi e che la popolazione sarà informata sulle procedure e sui tempi dei lavori.
### Procedura dei lavori
I lavori inizieranno con i muri di controriva sulla tratta Bioggio-Manno nella seconda metà di ottobre. Nei primi mesi dell’anno prossimo, si procederà con il pozzo di collegamento alla stazione ferroviaria a Besso e il portale lato ovest della galleria di Breganzona alla Crespera. Questi sono i primi passi di un progetto che mira a collegare il centro città di Lugano con una galleria di oltre due chilometri.
### Costo e tempistiche
Il costo complessivo del progetto è di 760 milioni di franchi, e l’obiettivo è consegnare l’opera nel 2035. Finora sono stati assegnati dieci mandati per un importo totale di quasi 45 milioni di franchi. Le procedure di approvazione del progetto sono terminate a giugno con la sentenza del Tribunale federale che ha negato l’effetto sospensivo all’unico ricorso ancora pendente.

Alla conferenza stampa mancava una figura politica. Al consigliere di Stato Claudio Zali sono state tolte le competenze del Dipartimento del territorio ora in mano al collega di Governo Raffaele De Rosa. Tuttavia, Diego Rodoni, direttore della Divisione delle costruzioni al Dipartimento del territorio, ha assicurato che le procedure sono state seguite correttamente e che i tecnici hanno continuato a lavorare indipendentemente dalle situazioni politiche.

item.description: Preliminary work for the Luganese tram-train will begin at the end of October 2026 on the Bioggio-Manno section.
